findings.recommendation: Load and validate the baseline inside the guarded operation, or add a dedicated catch that returns a precise structured failure such as 'The Gitleaks baseline is invalid.' Distinguish malformed baseline input from malformed scanner output in the reported reason.

findings.title: Staged file contents are corrupted by a text decoding and encoding round trip
findings.description: git show output is read through a StreamReader into a string and then written using text encoding. Files that are not valid UTF-8, contain a byte-order mark, or are binary will not be reproduced byte-for-byte in the temporary staged tree, which can cause missed or fabricated matches.
findings.recommendation: Capture git show stdout as bytes and copy those bytes directly to the destination file. Keep the separate text-capturing helper only for Git commands whose output is defined as textual path data.

grade.rationale: The implementation is compact and readable, but renaming a guideline can cause later silent data loss. Non-atomic uniqueness checks, catalogue-wide failure on one malformed file, and incomplete boundary validation further reduce robustness. Build analysis reported no findings; test coverage is unknown.

observations.summary: The primary defect is that Update changes the stored id without changing the filename, allowing a subsequent Create with the old id to overwrite the renamed guideline. Filesystem concurrency and malformed or null input handling also need improvement.

findings.title: Renaming a guideline leaves it vulnerable to silent overwrite
findings.description: Update writes the new id into the existing filename. For example, renaming id `foo` to `bar` leaves the definition in `foo.md`. A later Create for `foo` sees no existing definition with that id and writes `foo.md` with replacement enabled, silently deleting the renamed `bar` guideline.
findings.recommendation: Keep filenames synchronized with ids when renaming, using a collision-safe move or write-and-delete operation, or reject id changes explicitly. Ensure the operation cannot overwrite an unrelated destination.

findings.title: Check-then-write mutations can overwrite concurrent changes
findings.description: Create checks uniqueness by listing files and later calls a write path that explicitly replaces the destination. Two concurrent creates can both pass the check, after which the last move silently wins. Update has the same check-then-write exposure.
findings.recommendation: Make conflict detection part of the filesystem mutation, such as creating or moving without replacement for Create, and serialize mutations per repository or use an appropriate concurrency token for Update.

findings.title: One malformed guideline disables every catalogue operation
findings.description: Parsing occurs directly inside the deferred enumeration without per-file error handling. If any Markdown file is malformed or unreadable, List fails completely; because Create, Update, and Delete call List, that one file also prevents otherwise unrelated mutations.
findings.recommendation: Handle parsing failures per file and return structured diagnostics alongside valid entries, or throw a domain-specific exception that identifies the offending path. Mutation lookup should not require successfully parsing every unrelated file.

findings.title: Null kind or level entries cause incidental null-reference failures
findings.description: The public validation boundary invokes ToLowerInvariant on each collection element without checking for null. Runtime callers can still supply null despite nullable annotations, producing NullReferenceException instead of the documented argument-validation behavior.
findings.recommendation: Reject null or blank elements explicitly before normalization and include the affected parameter or field in the resulting ArgumentException.

grade.rationale: The aggregation rules are implemented clearly and consistently, with appropriate null guards and straightforward recursive composition. The main weakness is that WorstOf silently treats undefined ReviewState values as if they supplied no evidence, potentially producing a misleading result.

observations.summary: The implementation is concise, readable, and appears correct for the declared ReviewState values. One error-handling gap should be addressed so invalid or newly added enum values cannot be silently ignored. Test coverage is unknown because no coverage data was supplied.

findings.title: Undefined review states are silently treated as absent evidence
findings.description: WorstOf handles the three expected ReviewState values through conditional branches but has no fallback for an undefined numeric enum value. Such values can enter through casts, deserialization, corrupted data, or a future enum addition. They are silently ignored, so an input containing only an unsupported value returns NotReviewed and can misrepresent the underlying review status.
findings.recommendation: Use an exhaustive switch over ReviewState and throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException for unsupported values. This also forces future enum additions to receive an explicit precedence decision. Add tests covering every declared state, mixed-state precedence, empty input, and an undefined enum value.

grade.rationale: The class is concise and generally enforces document ownership and hierarchy constraints, but its collection exposure permits invariant-bypassing mutation, and some constructor and hierarchy validation is incomplete or coupled to enum representation.

observations.summary: The implementation is readable and mostly well structured. The principal correctness risk is returning mutable List instances as IReadOnlyList interfaces. Additional weaknesses are reliance on numeric enum adjacency and failure to validate physical metadata documented as file-only and inherently non-negative. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Read-only properties expose mutable backing lists
findings.description: Children and Exclusions are typed as IReadOnlyList, but their runtime values are the underlying List instances. A caller can cast either value back to List and mutate it directly, bypassing level checks, null checks, and exclusion deduplication. This can place the node in a state that its public mutation methods are intended to prevent.
findings.recommendation: Create and retain read-only wrappers, such as children.AsReadOnly() and exclusions.AsReadOnly(), or expose immutable collection snapshots so callers cannot recover the mutable backing lists.

findings.title: Hierarchy validation depends on enum numeric ordering
findings.description: AddChild defines the hierarchy relationship by casting ReviewLevel values to integers and adding one. Reordering enum members, assigning explicit nonconsecutive values, or passing undefined enum values can silently reject valid relationships or accept meaningless ones. The constructor also does not establish that Level is a defined value.
findings.recommendation: Validate ReviewLevel at construction and express permitted parent-child relationships explicitly, for example with a switch over the parent level or a centralized hierarchy transition function.

findings.title: Physical metadata invariants are not enforced
findings.description: The constructor accepts negative byte sizes and line counts, and it accepts these values for every review level even though the property documentation says physical source information is present only for file nodes. This allows semantically invalid nodes to be created and shifts validation to downstream consumers.
findings.recommendation: Reject negative SizeBytes and LineCount values and enforce or clearly relax the file-only constraint. If non-file nodes must sometimes carry these values, update the documentation to describe that behavior.

grade.rationale: The resolver is compact and deterministic in several important respects, but priority allocation can produce incorrect effective inputs, review-kind validation accepts invalid enum values, duplicate identifiers are not controlled, and the claimed YAML frontmatter support is only a fragile subset.

observations.summary: The implementation has a clear data model, deterministic per-directory ordering, explicit budget accounting, path-confinement checks, and useful omission metadata. Its main correctness risk is that global and project inputs are budgeted as separate groups rather than by their combined priority. Validation and parsing also admit ambiguous or misleading configurations. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Budget allocation does not honor priority across global and project inputs
findings.description: ReadDirectory sorts each scope independently, but Resolve concatenates all remaining global inputs before all project inputs. Consequently, a low-priority global input can consume the budget and truncate or entirely exclude a higher-priority project input. This makes Priority misleading and can omit the most important effective guidance.
findings.recommendation: After applying project overrides, sort the combined effective sequence by descending Priority with deterministic Id and Source tie-breakers before allocating the budget. If global-first behavior is intentional, represent scope precedence explicitly and document that Priority applies only within a scope.

findings.title: Review-kind validation accepts undefined numeric and composite enum values
findings.description: Enum.TryParse can succeed for numeric strings and comma-separated combinations even when the resulting value is not a declared ReviewKind member. Such input passes validation and is normalized to the original string, usually causing all kind-specific inputs to be filtered out instead of producing the advertised unsupported-kind error.
findings.recommendation: Capture the parsed value, require Enum.IsDefined, and normalize from the validated enum value rather than from the caller-provided string. Alternatively, validate against the exact supported textual names with an ordinal-ignore-case comparison.

findings.title: Duplicate effective input identifiers are silently retained
findings.description: projectIds is used only to suppress matching global inputs; it does not ensure uniqueness among project inputs or among non-overridden global inputs. Multiple files with the same case-insensitive Id can therefore be included, producing duplicate guideline headings and ambiguous override and hash semantics.
findings.recommendation: Validate identifiers for case-insensitive uniqueness within each scope, or within the final effective set, and throw an InputFormatException that identifies all conflicting source files. If multiple files per identifier are supported, model and document their merge order explicitly.

findings.title: The frontmatter parser does not implement the YAML syntax it claims to accept
findings.description: Frontmatter is parsed by splitting each non-empty line at the first colon and storing the raw scalar text. Valid YAML constructs such as block sequences, comments, escaped or quoted scalar identifiers, and multiline values are rejected or interpreted incorrectly; duplicate keys are silently overwritten. For example, a quoted id retains its quote characters and may fail to override the corresponding unquoted id.
findings.recommendation: Use a maintained YAML parser with a small strongly typed schema, reject unknown or duplicate fields where appropriate, and validate applicability values. If the intentionally supported format is not YAML, rename and document it as a restricted key-value syntax and reject unsupported constructs with precise errors.

findings.title: Budget truncation can split a Unicode surrogate pair
findings.description: The budget and slice operate on UTF-16 code units. If the boundary falls between the two code units of a supplementary Unicode character, IncludedContent ends with an unpaired surrogate. Subsequent UTF-8 conversion or prompt serialization may replace or reject the malformed character, so included-character accounting and effective hashing no longer reflect intact source text.
findings.recommendation: Move the truncation boundary backward when it would split a surrogate pair, or define and implement the budget in Unicode scalar values. Add boundary tests using supplementary characters immediately around the budget limit.

grade.rationale: The implementation is readable and builds successfully, but its identity fallback can merge distinct findings, ID normalization is collision-prone, malformed severities are silently downgraded, and validation does not adequately enforce the contract's semantic invariants.

observations.summary: The contract is organized clearly and uses deterministic serialization and hashing, but several boundary and identity behaviors can silently corrupt finding data. The most significant risk is that fallback fingerprints omit the affected unit and locations, allowing separate occurrences of the same rule and text to receive an identical identity.

findings.title: Fallback fingerprints can collapse distinct finding occurrences
findings.description: When `finding.Identity` is not already a canonical SHA-256 value, the fallback fingerprint contains only the rule ID and textual fields. It omits `UnitId`, `UnitPath`, locations, and the task-change subject. Two occurrences of the same rule with identical text but different affected files or units therefore receive the same fingerprint, which can cause downstream deduplication or tracking to treat separate findings as one.
findings.recommendation: Include stable occurrence identity—at minimum the unit identifier/path and normalized locations—in the canonical fingerprint input, or use a shared identity routine that defines the intended scope explicitly. Add tests covering identical rule text at multiple locations.

findings.title: Lossy ID normalization can produce duplicate IDs
findings.description: For inputs that normalize to a syntactically acceptable value, `NormalizeId` returns the lossy normalized text without incorporating the original value. Distinct identities such as `A B` and `a-b`, or strings differing only in discarded punctuation or case, consequently produce the same envelope ID.
findings.recommendation: Derive IDs from the canonical fingerprint or append a stable hash of the original identity whenever normalization changes it. Add collision tests for case, whitespace, punctuation, and truncation variants.

findings.title: Invalid severity values are silently downgraded to Info
findings.description: An unrecognized severity string is converted to `FindingSeverity.Info`. A typo or producer-version mismatch can therefore turn a critical finding into informational data without any error or diagnostic, materially changing review prioritization.
findings.recommendation: Reject unknown or blank severity values with a descriptive exception, or represent the conversion failure explicitly so the caller must choose a fallback. If compatibility requires a fallback, preserve the raw value and emit a diagnostic rather than silently lowering severity.

findings.title: Envelope validation leaves required semantic fields unchecked
findings.description: `Validate` checks the schema, presence of the locations collection, and one canonicalization string, but does not reject null or blank IDs, subjects, producer data, rule IDs, titles, descriptions, recommendations, or fingerprints, nor does it verify fingerprint syntax. JSON `required` metadata detects omitted properties but can still accept explicit null values for reference-typed properties. Serialization can likewise receive programmatically constructed envelopes with invalid values.
findings.recommendation: Centralize and enforce all contract invariants in `Validate`, including non-null/non-blank strings, subject and producer validity, location validity, recognized fingerprint canonicalization, and fingerprint format. Return field-specific `JsonException` messages and test both omitted and explicitly null JSON properties.

grade.rationale: The implementation is well structured and readable, but several data-selection and aggregation defects can materially misrepresent quality status, while malformed metadata and insufficient Markdown escaping weaken robustness.

observations.summary: The report builder has clear models, deterministic ordering, injectable time, and generally sensible serialization. However, disabled review kinds can still affect findings and gates, cross-kind coverage can be overstated, unknown finding classifications silently evade summaries and gates, malformed sidecars are not consistently handled, and Markdown fields can alter report structure. The supplied .NET build evidence reports no findings; test coverage remains unknown.

findings.title: Disabled review kinds still contribute findings and gate failures
findings.description: EnabledKinds restricts score construction and staleness scans, but CountFindings and the returned repository finding list consume every loaded observation. Consequently, a repository configured for only one kind can report and fail its gate because of findings from explicitly disabled kinds.
findings.recommendation: Filter observations to the normalized enabled-kind set before calculating finding counts and constructing RepositoryQualityReport.Findings, or explicitly separate all discovered observations from the enabled findings used by the scorecard and gate.

findings.title: Coverage treats a file reviewed in any kind as fully covered
findings.description: Files from every enabled-kind scan are merged, the denominator is deduplicated by path, and a path is counted as reviewed when any corresponding scan is non-missing. For example, a file that is fresh for code but missing for security is reported as one of one reviewed files and therefore 100% covered, despite only half of its required kind-specific reviews existing.
findings.recommendation: Define coverage over path-and-kind review units, or count a path as reviewed only when it is non-missing for every enabled kind. Expose separate per-kind coverage if file-level aggregate coverage is also useful.

findings.title: Unknown severity and state values silently evade summaries and gates
findings.description: ParseFinding accepts arbitrary severity and state strings. CountFindings only increments predefined names, and the gate ignores severities absent from SeverityRank and states other than open or accepted. A misspelled or unsupported classification can therefore be included in the total while disappearing from breakdowns and avoiding a configured failure threshold.
findings.recommendation: Validate and canonicalize severity and state during parsing, rejecting unsupported values with contextual metadata errors. Alternatively, introduce explicit unknown buckets and make the gate fail safely when an active finding has an unrecognized severity.

findings.title: Structurally malformed sidecars can escape error handling or abort trend reconstruction
findings.description: AsObject, AsArray, GetValue, and JsonElement.GetProperty can throw exceptions other than JsonException when valid JSON has an unexpected shape or missing property. Current metadata can therefore escape the contextual QualityReportException wrapper, while a historical sidecar missing kind can terminate trend generation despite the stated policy that malformed historical sidecars should be ignored.
findings.recommendation: Use type checks, TryGetProperty, and TryGetValue throughout sidecar parsing. Convert current-schema violations into a contextual QualityReportException, and catch all expected schema-shape exceptions for historical sidecars so they are skipped consistently.

findings.title: Markdown escaping does not protect report structure
findings.description: EscapeMarkdown only escapes vertical bars, although repository metadata supplies headings, list entries, table cells, locations, and other rendered text. Embedded newlines, carriage returns, backslashes, or Markdown control characters can break tables or create forged headings and findings in the generated Markdown report.
findings.recommendation: Use context-specific Markdown escaping and normalize or reject line breaks in inline fields. At minimum, escape backslashes and Markdown delimiters and replace CR/LF characters with safe inline whitespace before rendering headings, tables, and list items.

grade.rationale: The comparison is concise and deterministic for well-formed, uniquely fingerprinted active findings, but it conflates explicitly resolved findings with absent findings and silently resolves duplicate fingerprints by input order. These behaviors can produce misleading comparison results without warning.

observations.summary: The implementation is readable and structurally simple, with clear ordering and basic argument validation. Its main correctness risk is filtering resolved findings before comparison, which loses known state information and misclassifies reactivated findings. Duplicate fingerprints are also silently collapsed using the last enumerated item, making results depend on observation ordering.

findings.title: Resolved findings are conflated with findings absent from the candidate report
findings.description: Both snapshots discard every finding whose state is exactly "resolved" before fingerprints are aligned. Consequently, an active baseline finding that is explicitly present as resolved in the candidate is projected with CandidateState null, losing the known candidate state. Conversely, a fingerprint that is resolved in the baseline and active in the candidate is reported as New with BaselineState null rather than as a state transition. This makes absence, resolution, and reactivation indistinguishable and prevents DispositionChanged from representing transitions involving resolved.
findings.recommendation: Index all findings by fingerprint first, preserve their actual states, and classify transitions explicitly. If the public contract intentionally treats resolved entries as absent, document that null means “not active” rather than “not present” and add a separate classification or normalization step for reactivated findings.

findings.title: Duplicate fingerprints are silently resolved using input order
findings.description: Grouping by fingerprint and selecting group.Last() silently discards all other matching findings. If observations contain duplicate fingerprints with different states, severities, titles, or locations, comparison output depends on observation enumeration order rather than an explicit domain rule. Reordering otherwise equivalent observations can therefore change classification and projected details.
findings.recommendation: Enforce fingerprint uniqueness and fail with a descriptive validation error, or define and document a deterministic merge policy independent of observation order, such as aggregating locations and rejecting conflicting states or metadata.

grade.rationale: The data model and storage API are generally clear, but incomplete document validation, inconsistent safe-loading behavior, incorrect retention semantics, and unstable pagination can produce runtime failures or incorrect operational results.

observations.summary: The implementation is readable and uses sensible serialization and filename safeguards. Four correctness and error-handling issues remain, principally around accepting structurally invalid reports, leaking validation exceptions from LoadSafely, retaining more snapshots than documented, and using mutable offset-based trend cursors. Test coverage is unknown because no coverage evidence was supplied.

findings.title: Deserialization accepts incomplete report graphs
findings.description: Validate checks only the schema fields and three Run properties. System.Text.Json can supply null or default values for missing positional-record properties, so a document with a minimally valid Run can be returned even when Subject, Execution, Observations, Delta, Summary, or their nested collections are absent. Consumers such as the trend builder then dereference these values and can fail with NullReferenceException instead of rejecting the snapshot as corrupt.
findings.recommendation: Validate every required top-level and nested value during deserialization, including non-null collections and objects, allowed enum-like strings, numeric ranges, timestamps, and cross-field invariants. Alternatively, mark required JSON properties explicitly and convert all schema violations into JsonException.

findings.title: LoadSafely can throw for malformed snapshots
findings.description: Validation uses ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace for the run ID, while LoadSafely classifies only JsonException and InvalidDataException as corrupt. A snapshot containing an empty run ID therefore leaks ArgumentException, and a null Run can similarly leak NullReferenceException, contradicting the method's documented non-throwing behavior for corrupt files.
findings.recommendation: Make document validation consistently throw JsonException for malformed serialized content and ensure LoadSafely catches the complete, intentionally bounded set of corruption exceptions. Keep environmental I/O failures distinct if they should remain exceptional.

findings.title: Prune retains more unpinned snapshots than documented
findings.description: The documented policy is the newest keep snapshots plus every pinned baseline, but the implementation removes pinned reports before selecting the newest keep entries. If pinned reports occur within the newest keep snapshots, it retains keep unpinned reports in addition to them, preserving older unpinned snapshots that should fall outside the cutoff.
findings.recommendation: Order all reports first, take the newest keep reports, union that set with pinned reports, and delete everything outside the union. Add tests where zero, some, and all of the newest reports are pinned.

findings.title: Offset cursor can skip or duplicate trend entries
findings.description: The cursor is a numeric offset into a series ordered by mutable report data. If a new run is inserted, a run is removed, or a revision changes ordering between page requests, the same offset can repeat an already returned run or skip one that has not been returned.
findings.recommendation: Use an opaque keyset cursor containing the last point's complete deterministic sort key, such as FinishedAt and RunId, and fetch records strictly after that key. Version or sign the cursor if it is part of a public API.

grade.rationale: The implementation is compact and generally clear, but cross-instance read-modify-write races can silently lose pins, undermining the store's retention guarantee. Persisted documents also lack structural and version validation, and cleanup can obscure the original storage failure.

observations.summary: The store uses deterministic serialization, ordinal identifiers, per-instance locking, and temporary-file replacement. Its main weakness is that synchronization applies only to one object instance, so concurrent writers can overwrite each other's changes. Deserialized data should also be validated before use, and temporary-file cleanup should preserve the primary exception.

findings.title: Concurrent store instances can silently lose pin updates
findings.description: The gate protects only this QualityRunReportPinStore instance. Two instances or processes targeting the same repository can both load the same old set, modify it independently, and overwrite pins.json in sequence. The later move silently discards the earlier update, potentially allowing retention pruning to delete a run that an operator successfully pinned.
findings.recommendation: Coordinate the entire load-modify-persist transaction across instances and processes, for example with a repository-specific lock file acquired using exclusive file access and bounded retry handling. Reload the document only after acquiring that lock and retain the temporary-file replacement strategy for the final write.

findings.title: Loaded documents are used without schema or field validation
findings.description: Deserialization accepts any SchemaVersion and immediately passes PinnedRunIds to HashSet. A future or unsupported schema is therefore interpreted as the current format, while JSON containing a null pinnedRunIds value produces an indirect ArgumentNullException rather than a useful invalid-data error. This also makes the persisted schema version ineffective as a compatibility mechanism.
findings.recommendation: After deserialization, explicitly require the supported schema version and a non-null PinnedRunIds collection, throwing InvalidDataException with the file path and validation reason when either check fails. Consider wrapping JsonException similarly while preserving it as the inner exception.

findings.title: Temporary-file cleanup can mask the original persistence error
findings.description: If serialization, writing, flushing, or moving fails and deleting the temporary file also fails, the exception from File.Delete replaces the original exception. Callers then receive a less useful cleanup error and lose the cause of the failed persistence operation.
findings.recommendation: Preserve the primary exception when cleanup fails, such as by recording whether the try block failed and suppressing or reporting the secondary deletion failure without replacing it. Allow a deletion exception to propagate normally when cleanup itself is the only failure.

grade.rationale: The renderer is generally well structured and consistently HTML-encodes dynamic content, but incomplete Markdown escaping and defective SARIF range normalization can produce unsafe or invalid reports. Several smaller API-consistency and determinism issues remain.

observations.summary: The implementation provides useful Markdown, HTML, JSON, and SARIF representations with clear formatting and sensible finding ordering. The principal risks are report-integrity problems in Markdown and invalid SARIF regions for malformed or zero-based locations. Gate diagnostics can also overcount duplicated findings. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Markdown escaping does not protect report structure
findings.description: EscapeMarkdown only handles backslashes, table separators, and line breaks. Dynamic paths, identifiers, titles, evidence-derived values, and other fields can still contain backticks, brackets, emphasis markers, HTML, or link/image syntax. Backticks are particularly problematic where the escaped value is subsequently placed inside an inline-code span. Untrusted report content can therefore alter or forge the rendered Markdown presentation.
findings.recommendation: Use a Markdown escaping routine appropriate to each context. Escape inline-code values by choosing a safe backtick delimiter and padding rules, and escape or neutralize all Markdown metacharacters in ordinary text. Add tests containing backticks, links, images, HTML, emphasis, and list syntax.

findings.title: SARIF end coordinates can remain invalid after normalization
findings.description: The start line is clamped to one, but endLine is compared against the original, potentially non-positive start line. For example, startLine 0 and endLine 0 produce startLine 1 and endLine 0. End columns are likewise clamped only to one and can precede the start column on the same line. Such regions violate SARIF location ordering and may be rejected or misinterpreted by consumers.
findings.recommendation: Normalize the start coordinates first, then derive end coordinates from those normalized values. Ensure endLine is at least startLine and, when both positions are on the same line, ensure endColumn is valid relative to startColumn. Cover zero, negative, and reversed ranges with tests.

findings.title: FileExtension silently accepts unsupported format values
findings.description: Render throws for an unsupported QualityReportFormat value, while FileExtension returns "txt" for the same value. This inconsistent contract can cause callers to create a misleading output path before rendering fails and can conceal missing handling when new enum values are introduced.
findings.recommendation: Throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException in FileExtension as Render does. If a text fallback is intentionally supported, make it an explicit enum member and support it consistently in both methods.

findings.title: Severity gate counts duplicate finding fingerprints
findings.description: Report rendering deduplicates findings by fingerprint, but the severity gate queries every observation directly. If the same finding appears in multiple observations, the gate decision remains blocking but its diagnostic count is inflated and disagrees with the rendered report.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate the same deduplicated finding sequence used by the renderer, or extract a shared current/active-findings helper that both rendering and gate evaluation use. Add a test where two observations contain the same fingerprint.

findings.title: Cost formatting depends on the process culture
findings.description: The cost interpolation uses the current culture, whereas token counts and timestamps are explicitly formatted with invariant culture. Identical reports can therefore differ across machines, including use of a decimal comma, which reduces reproducibility and complicates snapshot tests or downstream parsing.
findings.recommendation: Format the cost with CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, preferably through FormattableString.Invariant or usage.Cost.Value.ToString("0.####", CultureInfo.InvariantCulture).

grade.rationale: The implementation is generally structured and deterministic, and the available .NET analyzer found no build issues. However, repository discovery can produce incomplete or incorrectly scoped Angular hierarchies, the Git subprocess can hang indefinitely, and the fallback ignore implementation differs materially from Git semantics.

observations.summary: The adapter design is readable, but several edge cases affect its core hierarchy output. The most important problems are workspace candidates escaping their declaring package directory, global suppression of alternate Angular discovery after finding any angular.json project, and unsafe synchronous handling of the Git subprocess. Test coverage is unknown; the unavailable ESLint result is not relevant evidence for this C# file.

findings.title: Nested workspace configurations can claim packages outside their directory
findings.description: RelativeRepositoryPath returns the original repository-relative path when the candidate is not beneath the workspace directory. That returned value is still tested against workspace globs, so broad patterns such as `*` or `**` can match an ancestor or sibling package. This creates false Angular project definitions and can suppress the generic adapter.
findings.recommendation: Reject candidates that are not descendants of the package.json directory before applying workspace patterns. Prefer a helper that returns failure for out-of-scope paths instead of returning the original path.

findings.title: One angular.json suppresses discovery in every other workspace
findings.description: As soon as any angular.json yields a project definition, discovery returns globally. In a repository containing an Angular CLI workspace alongside an independent package-workspace or TypeScript project-reference workspace, projects from the latter are never discovered. This conflicts with the comment that angular.json is authoritative for its own workspace.
findings.recommendation: Apply precedence per workspace boundary, or collect all discovery forms and remove only definitions shadowed by an angular.json governing the same directory tree.

findings.title: Git enumeration can hang indefinitely
findings.description: Both stdout and stderr are redirected, but only stdout is drained before WaitForExit. If Git fills the stderr pipe, it can block while the parent waits for stdout to close. There is also no timeout or cancellation path for a stalled Git process, so Build may never return.
findings.recommendation: Drain stdout and stderr concurrently, wait asynchronously with a bounded timeout or cancellation token, terminate the child on timeout, and then use the existing filesystem fallback.

findings.title: Fallback ignore handling does not preserve Git ignore semantics
findings.description: The custom parser trims lines and treats leading `#` and `!` unconditionally, so escaped literals and significant spaces are handled incorrectly. Its regex translation also omits supported constructs such as character ranges, and its sequential negation model can re-include a file beneath an excluded parent directory even though Git does not traverse that parent. When Git is unavailable, the hierarchy can therefore include ignored files or exclude tracked source unexpectedly.
findings.recommendation: Use a well-tested gitignore implementation. If custom parsing is retained, implement Git's escaping, whitespace, glob, directory-exclusion, and negation rules and add compatibility tests based on `git check-ignore`.

findings.title: Line counts are inflated for newline-terminated files
findings.description: CountLines initializes the result to one and increments for every LF byte. Consequently, a conventional file containing `text\n` is reported as two logical lines, while a CR-only file is always reported as one line. This can systematically distort hierarchy metrics.
findings.recommendation: Define the intended line-count convention explicitly and implement it consistently. For logical text lines, avoid adding a trailing empty line after a final terminator and recognize CR, LF, and CRLF without double-counting.

grade.rationale: The implementation is readable and deterministic, but it does not evaluate actual MSBuild compile items and derives C# structure with lossy regular expressions and incomplete symbol identities. These flaws can materially misrepresent repository hierarchy. File-system and parsing failures also abort the entire operation without partial diagnostics.

observations.summary: The builder has a clear high-level flow, stable hashing, deterministic ordering, and useful path-containment checks. Its principal correctness problem is treating every recursively discovered .cs file as part of each project instead of respecting evaluated MSBuild items. Regex-based namespace and function extraction then introduces false positives, omissions, and incorrect namespace attribution, while function deduplication collapses distinct members. Error isolation and filesystem abstractions are limited, reducing resilience and testability. Test coverage is unknown because no coverage evidence was supplied.

findings.title: Source discovery ignores evaluated MSBuild compile items
findings.description: Each module recursively claims every .cs file beneath the project directory. This includes files removed with Compile Remove, files belonging to nested projects, and other non-project sources, while omitting linked Compile items located outside the directory. A parent project can therefore absorb a nested project's files and report them again under the child module.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate each project with MSBuild and build the module from its resolved Compile items. Normalize and confine each resulting path to the repository, apply RepositoryScope to it, and deduplicate evaluated paths. If full evaluation is intentionally unsupported, define and enforce explicit project-boundary rules and surface the limitation.

findings.title: Regular expressions do not reliably identify C# namespaces and functions
findings.description: The namespace expression is not syntax-aware and returns only the first textual match, so namespace-like text in comments or strings can win and files containing multiple namespace declarations are assigned wholly to one namespace. The function expression can likewise match declaration-shaped text in comments while missing valid constructs such as generic methods, explicit-interface implementations, operators, and declarations affected by attributes or formatting. This makes the generated hierarchy dependent on source formatting rather than C# semantics.
findings.recommendation: Parse source with Roslyn and traverse the syntax tree or semantic model for namespace and callable-member declarations. Record the containing namespace and type for each symbol, and define explicitly whether constructors, local functions, accessors, and operators belong at the Function level.

findings.title: Function identity collapses distinct members with the same name
findings.description: The per-file deduplication key consists only of namespace and method name, and the same incomplete value is used in the canonical ID. Overloads and same-named methods declared by different types in one file are consequently represented by a single function node. Changing declaration order can also determine which declaration survives without preserving any signature information.
findings.recommendation: Use a canonical symbol identity containing at least the containing type, member kind, method name, generic arity, and parameter types. When semantic resolution is unavailable, include a normalized signature and source span so distinct declarations cannot collapse.

findings.title: A single unreadable or malformed artifact aborts the whole hierarchy build
findings.description: The existence check only handles a project disappearing before processing. Enumeration, solution parsing, namespace reads, and source reads can throw for malformed XML, invalid content paths, permissions, transient deletion, or I/O failures. These exceptions escape the public entry point, discarding otherwise valid hierarchy results from unrelated projects and solutions.
findings.recommendation: Define an explicit failure policy. For best-effort hierarchy generation, isolate processing per solution, project, and source file, convert recoverable failures into structured exclusions or diagnostics containing the affected path, and continue. For fatal failures, wrap exceptions with operation and path context while preserving the original exception.

grade.rationale: The implementation is readable and has a sensible per-repository synchronization model, but cache identity omits an input that directly affects the generated snapshot. Additional weaknesses in fallback invalidation, path comparison, process handling, and mutability can produce stale results or hangs in realistic environments.

observations.summary: The most important defect is that snapshots created with one InputResolver can be returned to callers using another resolver because resolver behavior is absent from the cache key. The Git-backed state calculation is generally thoughtful, and the supplied .NET analyzer reports no build findings, but the filesystem fallback can miss changes, Git execution can hang, and the public snapshot is not demonstrably immutable. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: InputResolver behavior is absent from the cache identity
findings.description: ReviewMetaDiscovery receives inputResolver and can therefore produce a different hierarchy for different resolver instances or configurations. The cache state includes only Git state, the global-input directory contents, and the character budget. Once a snapshot is cached, a later call using a different resolver—or no resolver—can receive the earlier snapshot without discovery running again.
findings.recommendation: Make resolver-dependent state an explicit part of the cache key, such as a stable resolver configuration/version token. If a resolver cannot provide stable identity, bypass this cache for custom resolvers or scope each cache instance to one immutable resolver configuration.

findings.title: The cached snapshot is only superficially immutable
findings.description: IReadOnlyList prevents mutation through that interface but does not make the underlying collection or its HierarchyNode elements immutable. The builder's hierarchy is stored and returned directly, so a caller that obtains mutable nodes or casts the underlying collection can alter the shared snapshot observed by later callers.
findings.recommendation: Freeze or deeply copy the hierarchy before caching it. Prefer immutable node types and an ImmutableArray<HierarchyNode>, or expose a detached read-only representation that contains no mutable collections or node state.

findings.title: Filesystem fallback can miss content changes
findings.description: When Git status is unavailable, file state is represented only by relative path, length, and LastWriteTimeUtc. Replacing content while preserving its length and timestamp leaves the state hash unchanged, so content-dependent discovery can return a stale cached snapshot.
findings.recommendation: Hash file contents in the fallback, as is already done for changed Git paths and global input files. If performance requires metadata shortcuts, document the weaker guarantee and use a validated content cache rather than treating metadata as definitive identity.

findings.title: Git execution can deadlock or wait indefinitely
findings.description: Standard error is redirected but never read. If Git writes enough diagnostic output to fill that pipe, Git blocks while the parent waits for standard output to close, causing ReadToEnd to wait forever. There is also no timeout or cancellation mechanism for a stalled Git process.
findings.recommendation: Drain standard output and standard error concurrently, impose a configurable timeout or accept a CancellationToken, and terminate the process tree on timeout. Preserve bounded stderr diagnostics so fallback causes can be observed or tested.

findings.title: Repository slot comparison is wrong on case-sensitive filesystems
findings.description: OrdinalIgnoreCase merges repository paths that differ only by case even on Linux and other case-sensitive filesystems. Such repositories share one slot; if their computed states match, one repository can receive the snapshot built for the other, and otherwise they continually evict each other's cached snapshot.
findings.recommendation: Use path comparison appropriate to the current platform, such as OrdinalIgnoreCase on Windows and Ordinal on case-sensitive platforms, after applying consistent path normalization.

findings.title: Fallback traversal does not exclude reparse-point directories
findings.description: Directory.EnumerateFiles with AllDirectories may traverse directory symlinks or junctions before the subsequent file filter runs. This can scan outside the repository, encounter cycles or inaccessible trees, and throw during cache-state computation. The filter also excludes only an exactly cased '.git' path segment.
findings.recommendation: Implement explicit directory traversal that skips reparse-point directories and Git metadata before descending. Use platform-appropriate name comparison and define how transient UnauthorizedAccessException and IOException failures should be surfaced or represented in state.

findings.title: Repository cache slots are never reclaimed
findings.description: Every distinct normalized repository path creates a CacheSlot that remains in the ConcurrentDictionary for the lifetime of the cache. A long-running service that examines many temporary or user-selected repositories will retain their keys, gates, and latest hierarchy snapshots indefinitely.
findings.recommendation: Add bounded eviction or expiration, provide an explicit invalidation/removal API, or scope RepositoryHierarchyCache to a known bounded repository set.

findings.title: External dependencies are hard-wired into cache logic
findings.description: Git process creation, filesystem enumeration, file reads, and stopwatch timing are invoked directly through static APIs. Deterministic tests for Git failures, hangs, filesystem races, and measurement values therefore require real processes and filesystem manipulation.
findings.recommendation: Extract narrow abstractions for repository state calculation and timing, or inject a state-provider delegate and clock. Keep production implementations backed by Git and the filesystem while allowing deterministic fault and concurrency tests.

grade.rationale: The implementation is generally readable and validates curated configuration carefully, but its rule evaluation does not fully preserve Git ignore semantics. In particular, negations can incorrectly re-include content below excluded parents, nested ignore files are discovered inside already excluded trees, and bracket-pattern translation is incomplete.

observations.summary: RepositoryScope has a clear structure and sensible precedence model, but several edge cases can produce a repository scope different from Git's. The deterministic .NET build reported no findings; test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Negations can re-include files beneath an excluded parent directory
findings.description: Every matching non-default rule simply replaces the previous winner. Consequently, rules such as `build/` followed by `!build/keep.cs` include `build/keep.cs`. Git does not permit a file to be re-included while one of its parent directories remains excluded, because Git does not traverse the excluded directory. This can make the derived scope include files Git still considers ignored.
findings.recommendation: Evaluate ignore state component-by-component and require every parent directory to be included before a descendant negation can take effect. Add tests for excluded parents, explicit parent re-inclusion, and nested ignore files.

findings.title: Ignore files are discovered inside built-in excluded trees
findings.description: The code recursively enumerates every `.gitignore` before applying exclusions, and the subsequent skip check considers only earlier GitIgnore rules. It therefore reads ignore files under built-in exclusions such as `.git`, `node_modules`, `bin`, and `obj`. Rules from those files are later than the defaults and can re-include content from a tree that repository traversal was intended to omit. Full recursive enumeration also adds avoidable cost in large dependency and build-output trees.
findings.recommendation: Walk directories incrementally and prune directories excluded by the effective rules before searching them for nested `.gitignore` files. If built-in exclusions are intentionally overridable, allow overrides only from an ignore file that was itself reachable under the parent scope.

findings.title: Bracket expressions are not translated with Git wildmatch semantics
findings.description: The parser treats the first `]` as the unconditional end of a character class and copies the remaining content directly into a .NET regex. Valid glob edge cases such as a leading literal `]` or escaped class members can therefore match differently from Git. Invalid ranges can also cause the Regex constructor to throw an uncontextualized RegexParseException while loading user-controlled rules.
findings.recommendation: Implement bracket-expression parsing explicitly according to Git wildmatch rules, escaping characters for .NET regex syntax as they are parsed. Validate compiled patterns and wrap failures with an InvalidDataException that identifies the curated rule index or `.gitignore` file and line.

grade.rationale: The implementation is compact and generally readable, with sensible validation and atomic file replacement, but the read-modify-write transaction is not protected across processes or aliased repository paths. Several malformed inputs are also accepted or reported inconsistently.

observations.summary: The store has a clear API and preserves rule ordering, but its atomicity guarantee is incomplete and input validation has edge cases. The most important improvement is coordinating the entire mutation across processes; validation should also reject malformed schema and reason values consistently and normalize patterns in an unambiguous order. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Mutation locking does not protect the file across processes or path aliases
findings.description: The gate is an in-memory object keyed by the textual full path. It serializes cooperating store instances in one process, but not another process, and distinct paths resolving to the same directory through junctions or symbolic links can receive different gates. Two callers can therefore read the same configuration and each replace it, silently losing one mutation. Atomic replacement prevents a partially written file but does not make the read-modify-write transaction atomic, contrary to the class documentation.
findings.recommendation: Hold an inter-process lock for the complete read-modify-write transaction, using a lock file or a named mutex derived from a canonical physical repository identity. Alternatively, add optimistic concurrency with a version/hash check and retry or reject conflicting writes. Clarify the documentation if multi-process coordination is intentionally unsupported.

findings.title: Include rules silently accept malformed reason values
findings.description: When a `reason` property exists but is not a JSON string, it is converted to null. Exclude rules subsequently fail validation, but include rules accept values such as numbers, objects, arrays, booleans, and null because their reason is discarded. This makes parsing less strict than the stated configuration contract and can silently erase malformed data on the next write.
findings.recommendation: If `reason` is present, explicitly require the permitted JSON kind and throw `InvalidDataException` otherwise. If JSON null is intentionally supported, handle that case explicitly rather than treating every non-string value as absent.

findings.title: Whitespace before a leading slash bypasses relative-pattern normalization
findings.description: The code removes leading slashes before trimming whitespace. Consequently, a value such as ` /src/**` becomes `/src/**`, while `/src/**` becomes `src/**`. The former passes validation but is stored in a form that is inconsistent with canonical candidate paths and may unexpectedly match nothing.
findings.recommendation: Trim surrounding whitespace before converting separators and removing leading slashes, or reject rooted patterns explicitly. Add tests covering whitespace around rooted and backslash-based patterns.

findings.title: Malformed schema types produce an inconsistent framework exception
findings.description: `GetString()` is called without first checking that `$schema` is a string. A numeric, object, array, or boolean schema value therefore throws `InvalidOperationException` instead of the contextual `InvalidDataException` used for other invalid configuration content.
findings.recommendation: When `$schema` is present, first require `JsonValueKind.String`, then compare its value and throw a single contextual `InvalidDataException` for either an invalid type or unsupported URI.

findings.title: Temporary-file cleanup can mask the original write failure
findings.description: If serialization, flushing, or moving the file fails and deleting the temporary file also fails, the exception from `File.Delete` replaces the original exception. This obscures the operation that actually caused the write to fail and makes diagnosis harder.
findings.recommendation: Preserve the primary exception when cleanup also fails, for example by performing best-effort cleanup in a guarded block and recording the cleanup failure separately. A filesystem abstraction would also make these failure paths testable.

grade.rationale: The implementation is concise and generally correct, with clear cancellation and failure result types. Its main weaknesses are that an optional observer can incorrectly turn an otherwise valid run into an agent failure, and the concrete runner construction leaves no practical unit-testing seam. The successful repository build supports basic compile-time correctness; test coverage remains unknown.

observations.summary: The agent streams output, records usage, preserves run metadata on failures, and distinguishes caller-requested cancellation from other exceptions. Error isolation around the observer and dependency injection for the runner would materially improve robustness and testability.

findings.title: Observer exceptions are misreported as coding-agent failures
findings.description: The optional event observer executes inside the same try block as the agent stream. If it throws, RunAsync stops consuming the stream and wraps the callback exception in ReviewAgentRunException, incorrectly indicating that the coding agent failed. For an OutputDelta, the observer also runs before the text is appended, so the triggering delta is omitted from the captured response and failure diagnostics.
findings.recommendation: Define an explicit observer-failure policy. If observation is non-critical, catch and report callback failures separately without interrupting stream processing, and append output before notification. If observer failures must abort the operation, introduce a distinct exception type so callers can distinguish instrumentation failures from agent failures.

findings.title: Runner construction prevents isolated unit testing
findings.description: The class constructs a concrete CliRunner internally and resolves its adapter during construction and again during execution. Tests cannot supply a deterministic fake stream or simulate completion, cancellation, and failure conditions without relying on the real runner and adapter configuration.
findings.recommendation: Inject a narrow runner or driver abstraction, or an adapter factory, while retaining a convenience constructor that creates CliRunner for production. Resolve the driver once when appropriate so construction and execution use the same dependency seam.

grade.rationale: The enum is concise, idiomatic, well documented, and correctly models three distinct review categories. No actionable defects were identified.

observations.summary: No issues found. The supplied file is a clear and maintainable enum declaration; the available .NET analyzer reported no findings, ESLint is not applicable to this C# file, and test coverage remains unknown.

grade.rationale: The enum is correct, concise, well documented, and appropriately scoped. No actionable defects are evident in the supplied file.

observations.summary: No issues found. The enum clearly represents the intended review hierarchy, uses conventional C# naming, and requires no local error handling. Test coverage is unknown and was not treated as absent; the available .NET build evidence reports no findings, while the unavailable ESLint check is irrelevant to this C# file.

grade.rationale: The data model is organized and serialization is deterministic, but the contract boundary accepts materially invalid documents, permits numeric enum representations, and can leak non-JSON exceptions. The shared mutable serializer options also make behavior order-dependent.

observations.summary: The implementation has a clear record-based structure and consistent property ordering, but validation is too narrow for a versioned metadata contract. Explicit nulls and contradictory grades can enter the system, enum encoding is less strict than the declared wire format suggests, malformed token types can produce inconsistent exceptions, and global options are publicly mutable. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Explicit nulls bypass required-member protection
findings.description: C# required members make JSON properties mandatory but do not reject an explicitly supplied null. Consequently, documents such as a current-schema document with "unit": null can pass ValidateContractVersion and be returned in an invalid state. The same input under the legacy schema dereferences document.Unit and throws NullReferenceException. Other required reference and collection properties have the same unvalidated-null problem.
findings.recommendation: Add centralized semantic validation that rejects null required objects, strings, and collections with JsonException before dereferencing them. Apply it consistently from every serialization and deserialization entry point, or use converters/schema validation that enforce non-null contract members.

findings.title: Contradictory grade values are accepted
findings.description: ReviewGrade independently exposes an unrestricted integer score and a band, while contract validation checks neither. A document can therefore deserialize and serialize with values such as score 100 and band F, or with a score outside 0–100, leaving consumers with conflicting review results.
findings.recommendation: Validate that scores are within 0–100 and that each band matches its defined score interval. Apply the validation to the overall grade and every aspect grade, and add boundary and mismatch tests.

findings.title: String enum converter still accepts numeric enum values
findings.description: JsonStringEnumConverter permits integer values by default. Metadata can therefore contain numeric values for most enums, including undefined values such as 999, despite serialization and the specialized GradeBand converter presenting enums as named strings. This weakens wire-format validation and can pass invalid states to downstream switches.
findings.recommendation: Construct the converter with allowIntegerValues set to false, and add tests proving that numeric and undefined enum values are rejected with JsonException.

findings.title: Converters leak InvalidOperationException for wrong token types
findings.description: Both custom converters call Utf8JsonReader.GetString without first checking that the token is a string. For numeric, object, or array tokens, GetString can throw InvalidOperationException rather than the JsonException used for other contract violations, making malformed-input handling inconsistent for callers.
findings.recommendation: Check reader.TokenType against JsonTokenType.String before calling GetString and throw a field-appropriate JsonException when it differs. Avoid naming every timestamp error reviewedAt because the converter also handles thread timestamps.

findings.title: Serializer options are exposed as mutable global state
findings.description: The public Options property returns the singleton JsonSerializerOptions instance used internally. A caller can modify it before its first serialization, changing contract behavior globally; after first use the same mutation instead throws because the options become read-only. This creates initialization- and test-order-dependent behavior.
findings.recommendation: Keep the internal singleton private. If callers need options, expose a factory or return a copy while ensuring Serialize, Deserialize, LoadAsync, and SaveAsync always use an encapsulated immutable configuration.

grade.rationale: The core matching and hashing flow is understandable, but discovery is fragile: one malformed or inaccessible sidecar can terminate the entire operation, policy drift can be skipped, and aggregate-member paths bypass the confinement checks applied to ordinary file inputs.

observations.summary: The implementation has a clear overall structure, but its failure isolation and validation are insufficient for repository-wide discovery. The most important improvements are handling sidecars independently, checking policy hashes even when subject inputs are absent, and applying repository confinement consistently.

findings.title: One bad sidecar can abort discovery for the entire repository
findings.description: Each candidate is read, parsed, and traversed without per-file error isolation. Invalid JSON, a non-object root, incorrect property types, a disappearing file, or an inaccessible directory/file can throw JsonException, InvalidOperationException, IOException, or UnauthorizedAccessException and prevent later valid sidecars from being attached.
findings.recommendation: Process each candidate behind a narrow per-file exception boundary, validate JsonElement.ValueKind before accessing properties or enumerating arrays, and expose diagnostics for rejected sidecars. Also define how directory-enumeration failures should be reported or skipped rather than allowing an incidental repository file to terminate discovery.

findings.title: Missing subjectInputs suppresses policy-drift detection
findings.description: When subjectInputs is absent, DetermineState returns Current immediately. Consequently, a document that still contains reviewInputs.effectiveHash is never compared with the current resolved review inputs and can be classified as current despite policy changes.
findings.recommendation: Treat an absent subjectInputs property as an empty subject-input collection and continue to the reviewInputs hash comparison. If absence instead denotes a legacy schema, make that compatibility rule explicit and validate the document version before returning Current.

findings.title: Aggregate member files bypass repository confinement
findings.description: The aggregate-members branch resolves and reads every file-node path directly. Unlike the normal file and aggregate-control branch, it does not call IsConfinedFile first. A hierarchy node with an absolute path, parent traversal, missing file, or reparse-point path can therefore read outside the repository or throw and abort discovery.
findings.recommendation: Resolve each aggregate member path, require IsConfinedFile(root, path) before hashing it, and return Stale or a distinct invalid state when any member is unavailable or escapes the repository. Keep the path used in the manifest canonical and repository-relative.

findings.title: Sidecar identification examines the entire path instead of the filename
findings.description: The marker check is applied to the absolute path. If any parent directory contains '.review-meta.', every JSON file beneath that directory is treated as a candidate sidecar, which can produce false positives and amplify parsing failures.
findings.recommendation: Apply the marker check to Path.GetFileName(path), or use a filename pattern that precisely defines the supported sidecar naming convention.

grade.rationale: The type is concise, immutable, and validates required strings and the explicitly forbidden state. Its main weakness is that undefined enum values can bypass the intended domain invariants and reach downstream aggregation.

observations.summary: Well-structured value object with clear documentation and straightforward guard clauses. Add validation for undefined ReviewKind and ReviewState values; test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Undefined enum values bypass constructor invariants
findings.description: The constructor rejects only ReviewState.NotReviewed and does not verify that state is a defined ReviewState value. It also accepts any numeric value cast to ReviewKind. Such values can enter through casts, parsing, or deserialization and then be consumed by aggregation as though they represented valid metadata.
findings.recommendation: Validate both enum arguments against their supported values, for example with Enum.IsDefined, before assigning them. Add constructor tests covering undefined numeric values as well as NotReviewed and every supported value.

grade.rationale: The catalog is well documented and mostly defensive, but recommendation behavior can silently diverge from the synchronized policy, input mistakes can weaken correctness floors, and one advertised routing band is unreachable.

observations.summary: The resolution and floor-comparison paths are generally clear, but the recommendation path duplicates policy data in code instead of consuming it. Three correctness issues and one testability limitation should be addressed before relying on this as a fully policy-governed router.

findings.title: Recommendations duplicate route definitions instead of using the synchronized policy
findings.description: Only route ranks are loaded from the policy. The model ID, thinking level, and capability tier returned by Recommend are hard-coded for each route ID. If the synchronized policy changes any of those fields while retaining the route ID, loading succeeds but Recommend silently returns the old route, potentially selecting an unavailable model or violating the policy's intended correctness floor.
findings.recommendation: Load a complete route descriptor for each core-task route, validate its model and thinking level against the catalog, and construct both scored and floor recommendations from those descriptors. Keep only score-to-route-ID decisions in code.

findings.title: Invalid review kinds can bypass specialized scoring and floors
findings.description: Recommend dereferences kind without a null check and treats every value other than the exact strings "security" and "performance" as a generic review. A null value therefore causes an incidental NullReferenceException, while a misspelling such as "securty" silently loses the security score and SolXhigh correctness floor. Undefined ReviewLevel enum values are likewise accepted as non-aggregate scopes.
findings.recommendation: Represent review kind with a validated enum or explicitly whitelist supported normalized values and throw a descriptive ArgumentException for null or unknown input. Validate ReviewLevel with Enum.IsDefined before scoring.

findings.title: The Luna score band is unreachable for valid inputs
findings.description: With files greater than zero, the minimum possible score is 28: generic kind (10), one file (4), non-aggregate scope (4), generic adjustment (5), and the final constant (5). Consequently the <=20 Luna branch can never be selected, despite Luna being declared as a recommendable route and the documented lightest floor.
findings.recommendation: Recalibrate the weights or score thresholds so the intended small-review route is reachable, or remove the dead band and document that Terra is the minimum scored recommendation. Add boundary tests for every score band.

findings.title: Policy validation cannot be tested with controlled catalog inputs
findings.description: Construction always reads three fixed manifest resources through a private static loader. This makes important failure paths—missing fields, mismatched route definitions, unknown thinking levels, duplicate aliases, and malformed fallback declarations—difficult to cover without building alternate assemblies or using reflection.
findings.recommendation: Add an internal constructor or loader abstraction that accepts streams or parsed documents, while retaining the public constructor as the embedded-resource production path. Unit-test both valid snapshots and each validation failure independently.

grade.rationale: The file contains a compile-blocking malformed string literal and multiple prompt-construction defects that can corrupt supplied content or permit it to escape its intended data section. The overall design is concise, but these correctness and trust-boundary failures prevent reliable use.

observations.summary: The implementation is compact and mostly readable, but it cannot compile as supplied. Its chained global replacements also mishandle the two guideline values and transform tokens occurring inside already-inserted file content, defeating the randomized content boundary. Additional evidence fields are appended without robust structural delimiting or validation, allowing untrusted text to alter the generated prompt.

findings.title: Malformed string literal prevents the project from compiling
findings.description: The first argument to `Replace` contains unescaped quotation marks (`"{"verdict"...` as source text), so the C# parser terminates the string after the opening brace and treats the remaining text as invalid syntax. Consequently, this class cannot be compiled as supplied. The prior `dotnet-build` evidence reports no findings, but that repository-level result is inconsistent with the reviewed content and does not negate the directly observable syntax error.
findings.recommendation: Encode the JSON placeholder with a raw string literal such as `"""{"verdict":"pass","sensors":[]}"""`, or escape every embedded quotation mark in a conventional string literal. Add a compilation test covering this source and a prompt-generation test for security evidence replacement.

findings.title: Global and project guidelines cannot be populated independently
findings.description: Both calls replace the same text, `(none supplied)`, across the entire prompt. The first call replaces every occurrence, leaving nothing for the second call. If global guidelines are supplied, they therefore occupy both guideline sections and project guidelines are ignored; if global guidelines are absent, the first replacement is effectively a no-op and the project value can populate both sections.
findings.recommendation: Give each template field a unique token, such as `{{GLOBAL_GUIDELINES}}` and `{{PROJECT_GUIDELINES}}`, and replace each token exactly once. Add tests for all four supplied/absent combinations.

findings.title: Later replacements can rewrite file content and forge its randomized boundary
findings.description: File content is inserted before several global replacements run. Any later search text appearing in the reviewed file—including `(none supplied)`, the security-scope sentence, or the fixed `QS-CONTENT-24b42f70ebd2c2672b65d949dfdb34fd` token—is consequently rewritten. In particular, repository content can include that publicly known fixed token; the final replacement converts it into the freshly generated boundary, allowing the content to reproduce a supposedly unpredictable closing marker and escape its data region.
findings.recommendation: Render the template without performing replacements over already-inserted values. For example, replace all unique template tokens in one token-aware pass, or generate the boundary first and interpolate values only after the template structure is finalized. Ensure the boundary token found inside `fileContent` is never transformed, and test adversarial content containing every template token and delimiter.

findings.title: Evidence values are inserted without a robust content boundary
findings.description: Security, coverage, deterministic-analyzer, and thread data can contain prompt syntax. The JSON code fences do not provide isolation because a string can contain a closing fence and new headings, while coverage evidence is appended as unrestricted text. `deterministicEvidence` and `securitySensorEvidence` are accepted as strings without JSON parsing, and JSON serialization of `openThreads` does not prevent Markdown fence termination. Repository-controlled analyzer messages or persistent thread bodies can therefore alter instructions seen by the reviewer.
findings.recommendation: Treat every evidence value as untrusted data. Parse JSON inputs into `JsonNode` values and serialize them canonically, then enclose all dynamic evidence in independently generated, non-rewritten boundaries with explicit instructions that its contents are data. Avoid Markdown fences as the sole trust boundary and add injection-focused tests using backticks, headings, and boundary-like strings.

grade.rationale: The parser validates the core review structure well, including grades, aspect references, severities, positions, and provenance restrictions. However, several malformed JSON shapes are either silently accepted or escape through unexpected exception types, and location ranges are not checked for logical ordering.

observations.summary: Core validation is clear and reasonably maintainable, but error handling is inconsistent for non-object nodes, optional properties can bypass type validation, and inverted source ranges are accepted. Build analyzer evidence reported no .NET findings; test coverage remains unknown.

findings.title: Non-object JSON roots escape the parser's exception contract
findings.description: JsonNode.AsObject() throws InvalidOperationException when the parsed root is an array or scalar, but the catch block handles only JsonException. Consequently, valid JSON with the wrong shape does not produce the documented domain-specific ReviewResponseException. The same AsObject pattern is also used for nested aspects, findings, locations, and thread updates.
findings.recommendation: Check node types with pattern matching, such as `node is JsonObject root`, or catch and wrap InvalidOperationException at the parsing boundary. Apply the same approach to nested object elements so every malformed response consistently raises ReviewResponseException.

findings.title: Optional properties accept null, arrays, and objects
findings.description: The fingerprint and status validators run only when the property value is a JsonValue. If either property is present as null, an array, or an object, its validation is skipped and the malformed response is accepted.
findings.recommendation: When an optional property is present, require it to be a JsonValue containing a string before validating its allowed format or values. Distinguish property absence from a present value of the wrong JSON type.

findings.title: Malformed threadUpdates values are silently ignored
findings.description: Thread updates are validated only when the property happens to be a JsonArray. A present null, string, number, or object is treated the same as an absent property, allowing an invalid top-level response shape to pass.
findings.recommendation: If the root contains `threadUpdates`, require its value to be a JsonArray and reject every other JSON type. Skip validation only when the property is genuinely absent.

findings.title: Location ranges may end before they start
findings.description: Start and end positions are independently checked for positive line and column values, but their relative ordering is never validated. The parser therefore accepts impossible ranges whose end precedes their start.
findings.recommendation: After validating both positions, compare them lexicographically by line and then column, rejecting a range when its end is earlier than its start.

grade.rationale: The runner is generally well structured, but several orchestration defects can misattribute reviewed content, accept stale results, or leave persistent review state inconsistent. Output-path handling and exception preservation also need stronger defenses.

observations.summary: The implementation has clear responsibilities and useful dependency injection, and the available dotnet-build evidence reports no findings. However, prompt construction and hashing do not use one immutable subject snapshot, freshness omits multiple prompt-affecting inputs, metadata output paths are not secured against traversal or repository-controlled reparse points, and multi-file persistence is not transactional. Test coverage is unknown, and the unavailable ESLint result is not relevant evidence about this C# file.

findings.title: Prompt content and reviewed hash come from different filesystem snapshots
findings.description: PreparePromptAsync reads the subject content and constructs the prompt before PrepareSubjectAsync hashes the files. A file change between those operations means the agent reviews the earlier content while reviewedHash describes the later content. The second hash check cannot detect this if the file remains at the later version. There is another window after the final hash check in which ReadSubjectContentsAsync can read yet another version for finding identity assignment.
findings.recommendation: Read every subject into a single immutable byte/content snapshot, derive the prompt, subject hashes, and finding identities from that snapshot, and compare current filesystem hashes with the snapshot immediately before committing metadata.
