findings.title: Freshness ignores prompt-affecting review inputs
findings.description: reviewInputsHash includes resolved InputResolver inputs and the template hash, but omits request-supplied global and project guidelines, security sensor evidence, deterministic evidence, coverage evidence, and open-thread context even though those values affect the prompt or resulting metadata. With unchanged source files, a non-forced run can therefore reuse a review produced from materially different instructions or evidence.
findings.recommendation: Compute freshness from a canonical manifest containing every semantically relevant prompt and result input, including combined guidelines, sensor configurations and result hashes, deterministic evidence, coverage evidence, and any thread state intended to trigger reconsideration.

findings.title: Metadata output paths are not containment- or reparse-point checked
findings.description: The metadata path incorporates the unconstrained Kind string and is passed directly to directory creation and an overwrite move. Separators and parent segments in Kind can alter the destination hierarchy. Even with a normal kind, a repository-controlled .quality directory can be a symbolic link or junction because EnsureContained is only applied to input paths. Reviews of an untrusted repository can consequently write or overwrite files outside the repository.
findings.recommendation: Restrict Kind to a validated enum or strict allowlist, construct filenames only from safe fixed tokens, and validate the resolved output path and every existing parent against repository containment and reparse points immediately before both temporary-file creation and replacement.

findings.title: Finding state is committed before review metadata
findings.description: MergeReviewAsync can persist lifecycle-state changes before the metadata temporary file is written and moved into place. Cancellation, serialization, disk, or move failures after the merge leave finding state representing a review that was never committed. Conversely, simply reversing the order would permit metadata without corresponding state, so the two resources require an explicit consistency mechanism.
findings.recommendation: Commit metadata and finding-state changes through a transaction-like protocol, such as staging both files followed by coordinated atomic replacements and recovery markers, or redesign the state store so the committed metadata revision is the authoritative unit and incomplete revisions can be detected and repaired.

findings.title: Usage persistence can replace the original agent exception
findings.description: Both agent-exception handlers await RecordUsageAsync before rethrowing. If ledger persistence or the usage callback throws, callers receive that secondary exception instead of the ReviewAgentRunException or ReviewAgentRunCanceledException that explains the failed run. The callback can similarly turn an otherwise successful agent run into a failed review after usage has already been persisted.
findings.recommendation: Preserve the original exception and treat accounting or observer failures separately. Log or aggregate persistence failures without losing the agent failure, and isolate the optional callback so observer exceptions cannot alter the review lifecycle unless that behavior is an explicit contract.

findings.title: Architecture-aspect enforcement depends on a fragile substring
findings.description: The project-review validation searches only request.ProjectGuidelines for the exact text id "architecture". It does not inspect resolved project guidelines included by InputResolver, and harmless formatting differences can bypass the check while unrelated prose containing the substring can trigger it. The response contract therefore varies according to an unreliable textual heuristic.
findings.recommendation: Represent required aspects as structured configuration produced while resolving guidelines, or enforce the architecture aspect unconditionally for project-level code reviews if it is part of that review schema. Validate against the structured requirement set rather than searching raw text.

grade.rationale: The implementation is concise and uses deterministic JSON property ordering, ordinal comparisons, strict decoding, domain separation, and SHA-256 appropriately. However, canonicalization is incomplete when logical identifiers are duplicated, file hashing creates several full-size in-memory representations, and the manifest hash uses a different textual format from the other public hash methods.

observations.summary: The core hashing logic is understandable and generally sound, but two canonicalization edge cases and one scalability concern should be addressed. Test coverage is unknown, so no coverage-based conclusion was drawn.

findings.title: Canonical ordering is incomplete for duplicate identifiers
findings.description: The manifest sorts inputs only by path and selector, and the aggregate sorts members only by unit ID. If two entries share those sort keys but differ in content hash, path, or subject hash, LINQ's stable sort preserves their original relative order. Consequently, two permutations of the same logical collection can produce different hashes, despite the evident intent to canonicalize collection order.
findings.recommendation: Either reject duplicate logical identifiers explicitly or establish a total order by adding every serialized value that can differ as an ordinal tie-breaker. Add permutation tests containing duplicate primary sort keys with different payloads.

findings.title: File hashing creates multiple full-size representations in memory
findings.description: The method loads the complete file into a byte array, decodes it into a string, may allocate another string during newline normalization, and finally creates another UTF-8 byte array. A sufficiently large review subject can therefore cause disproportionate memory use or an OutOfMemoryException instead of producing a hash reliably.
findings.recommendation: Decode incrementally with a BOM-aware StreamReader or decoder, normalize line endings across buffer boundaries, and feed normalized UTF-8 data into IncrementalHash. If file sizes are intentionally bounded elsewhere, enforce and document that limit at this boundary.

findings.title: Manifest hashes use a different textual format from other hashes
findings.description: ComputeFileContentHashAsync and ComputeAggregateMembersHash return values prefixed with "sha256:", while ComputeManifestHash returns only lowercase hexadecimal characters. This makes similarly named public methods easy to misuse and can cause mismatches when their results are stored or compared through a common hash field.
findings.recommendation: Adopt one documented representation across all three methods, preferably the algorithm-qualified form, or introduce distinct value types and clearly document why manifest hashes intentionally use a different wire format. Account for compatibility if persisted hashes already exist.

grade.rationale: The implementation has a serious cross-file anchor-healing defect and several robustness gaps around malformed agent and persisted JSON data. The core merge and line-relocation logic is understandable, but validation, resource lifecycle, and clock handling need improvement.

observations.summary: The most significant issue is that fingerprint-based healing can attach a detached thread to content from a different file. Public methods also assume structurally valid JSON and ranges, allowing malformed model responses or metadata to terminate processing or produce misleading anchors. Test coverage is unknown because no coverage data was supplied.

findings.title: Fingerprint healing can relocate a thread using the wrong file
findings.description: The method examines every detached thread and matches only its fingerprint against findings containing a location for `relativePath`. It never verifies that the thread anchor's own `path` equals `relativePath`. A detached thread belonging to another file can therefore receive a range and context hash computed from the current file while retaining its original path, corrupting the anchor metadata.
findings.recommendation: Before attempting fingerprint lookup, require the anchor path to equal `relativePath` using the same explicit comparison semantics as `LoadAndHeal`. Prefer indexing candidates by both fingerprint and normalized path.

findings.title: Malformed agent updates can terminate the entire update operation
findings.description: Agent-produced update nodes and required properties are accessed through null-forgiving operators and strict conversions. A null or non-object element, missing or non-string `threadId` or `body`, or a thread with malformed `entries` causes an exception, potentially discarding all otherwise valid updates in the response.
findings.recommendation: Validate each update and target thread with non-throwing type checks. Skip invalid records while returning or recording structured diagnostics, and validate status and reply identifiers against the expected schema before mutation.

findings.title: Corrupt or partially written metadata is not handled safely
findings.description: Reading and parsing the metadata file can throw for invalid JSON, an unexpected root type, I/O races, or access failures. Later merge indexing also assumes every thread has a unique string ID. Consequently, one damaged or partially written metadata file can abort review processing rather than being treated as recoverable state.
findings.recommendation: Centralize metadata deserialization and schema validation, catch the specific JSON and I/O failures that can be recovered from, and report a diagnostic or quarantine the invalid file. Build indexes with explicit handling for missing and duplicate IDs instead of `ToDictionary` assumptions.

findings.title: TryRange accepts semantically invalid source ranges
findings.description: `TryRange` verifies only that four integer values can be extracted. It accepts non-positive lines or columns, an end before the start, and other invalid combinations. Downstream code clamps lines and forces the span to at least one line, so corrupt data can be converted into an apparently anchored or healed range instead of being detached.
findings.recommendation: Reject ranges unless line and column values are positive and the end position is not before the start position. Keep invalid persisted ranges detached rather than silently clamping them into the document.

findings.title: The write-lock registry grows for the lifetime of the process
findings.description: Every distinct full metadata path permanently adds a `SemaphoreSlim` to the static dictionary. Processes that review many transient repositories or metadata paths accumulate locks that are never removed or disposed.
findings.recommendation: Encapsulate lock acquisition in a scoped lease and remove idle entries with reference counting, or use a bounded keyed-lock implementation that safely handles entry lifecycle and disposal.

findings.title: Healing timestamps bypass the injectable operation time
findings.description: Update creation accepts a caller-supplied time, but both healing paths read `DateTime.UtcNow` directly. This inconsistency makes deterministic tests harder and can give one logical operation timestamps from different clock sources.
findings.recommendation: Pass a `DateTimeOffset now` or an injected `TimeProvider` through both healing paths and use it consistently for all timestamps.

grade.rationale: The resolver is concise and generally correct, with deterministic precedence and useful validation. Its main weaknesses are misleading override provenance and incomplete validation of externally supplied override arrays.

observations.summary: The implementation is well structured and readable, but global severity overrides are presented as project overrides, null override elements can escape the intended JsonException contract, and duplicate entries within one override file are silently resolved by order. Build evidence reported no .NET findings; test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Global severity overrides are labeled as project overrides
findings.description: Content() emits the fixed label 'Project override' whenever severity was overridden. For an override loaded from the global inputs directory, this gives the review model false provenance and can make centrally managed policy appear repository-specific.
findings.recommendation: Derive the label from the recorded source or add an explicit override-scope value such as 'global' or 'project' to ResolvedRule and render the corresponding wording.

findings.title: Null override entries cause an unintended NullReferenceException
findings.description: System.Text.Json can populate a collection with a null element despite its non-nullable generic annotation. Apply dereferences entry immediately, so an overrides array containing null fails with NullReferenceException instead of the source-aware JsonException used for other contract violations.
findings.recommendation: Check entry for null before accessing its properties and throw a JsonException that identifies the override file and invalid array entry. Consider applying equivalent defensive validation to catalogue entries.

findings.title: Duplicate rule overrides within one file silently overwrite each other
findings.description: Assignments to overridesById intentionally implement precedence between global and project files, but they also make repeated IDs inside a single file silently last-write-wins. This can conceal configuration mistakes and makes behavior depend on array ordering.
findings.recommendation: Validate that IDs are unique within each RuleOverrideDocument before applying it, while retaining the dictionary replacement behavior between separately layered documents.

grade.rationale: The implementation is thoughtfully structured and supports dependency injection, deterministic ordering, containment checks, and bounded evidence. However, several valid SARIF constructs are interpreted incorrectly, suppressed results are emitted as active findings, and some malformed reports escape the intended unavailable-result error path.

observations.summary: The sensor has a solid overall design, but SARIF URI decoding, tool-component resolution, suppression handling, exception normalization, and command tokenization need correction. The supplied build evidence reports no findings; ESLint was unavailable because its local module was missing. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Accepted SARIF suppressions are emitted as active findings
findings.description: The result filter excludes only kind values pass and notApplicable. A failing result whose suppressions array contains an accepted suppression is therefore mapped into a normal ReviewFinding, even though the SARIF producer or user has explicitly suppressed it. This can reintroduce waived diagnostics and distort review results.
findings.recommendation: Inspect result.suppressions before mapping the result and omit results with an accepted suppression, or expose a clearly documented option to include suppressed results while preserving their suppression state.

findings.title: Name-only tool-component references resolve against the driver
findings.description: SARIF toolComponent references can identify an extension by name without supplying an index. The implementation ignores the name and converts a missing index into component zero, which represents the driver in the local component list. The result can consequently inherit the wrong rule title, severity, help text, and properties.
findings.recommendation: Represent components with their tool-component identity and resolve toolComponent by index when present, otherwise by its name or GUID. Validate that multiple supplied identifiers refer to the same component.

findings.title: Artifact URIs are decoded before URI resolution
findings.description: ResolvePath percent-decodes the entire URI reference before parsing or combining it with a base URI. Encoded reserved characters then acquire URI syntax: for example, foo%23bar.cs becomes foo#bar.cs, so resolution against a file base treats bar.cs as a fragment and maps the finding to foo. Encoded slashes and question marks can similarly change path structure or query handling.
findings.recommendation: Normalize separators without decoding reserved characters, resolve the original escaped URI reference against its base, and obtain the decoded filesystem path from the resulting file URI. Decode individual path components only when handling a non-URI filesystem representation.

findings.title: URI and path errors can escape the unavailable-result contract
findings.description: The report-ingestion catch filter handles JSON, I/O, invalid-data, and invalid-operation exceptions, but location resolution can also throw UriFormatException, ArgumentException, or NotSupportedException while unescaping, constructing URIs, or normalizing paths. Such a report faults RunAsync instead of returning a SensorScanResult marked unavailable like other invalid reports.
findings.recommendation: Catch the expected URI and path-format exception types around parsing and convert them to the same unavailable result. Prefer wrapping per-report structural failures in InvalidDataException so callers see one consistent failure contract.

findings.title: The command splitter drops explicitly empty arguments
findings.description: Quote characters change parser state but do not mark a token as present, and tokens are emitted only when the buffer contains characters. Consequently, commands containing "" or '' lose that argument entirely. This changes positional arguments for analyzers that require an explicit empty value.
findings.recommendation: Track whether a token has started independently from the buffer length, and emit the token when whitespace or end-of-input is reached even when its quoted content is empty. Add tests for empty quoted arguments, adjacent quoted segments, whitespace, and escaped quotes.

grade.rationale: The declarations are concise and compile successfully, but several public models permit contradictory or malformed states. Duplicate representations of availability, findings, counts, and provenance weaken correctness and make consumers responsible for maintaining invariants.

observations.summary: The file is readable and structurally simple, and the available .NET build analyzer reported no findings. The main risks are representational: requests can encode incompatible mode/range combinations, reports can disagree about availability, results duplicate report data, and timestamps are weakly typed. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Request permits incompatible mode and range combinations
findings.description: `Mode` and `Range` are independent constructor parameters, so callers can create `Range` mode requests without a range or attach a range to `Repository` or `Staged` modes. Every downstream consumer must detect these invalid combinations consistently.
findings.recommendation: Represent each scan mode with a distinct validated request type, or add construction-time validation that requires a non-empty range only for `SecurityScanMode.Range` and rejects it for other modes.

findings.title: Availability state has three unsynchronized representations
findings.description: `Verdict`, `Available`, and `UnavailableReason` can contradict one another, such as `Available == true` with an `Unavailable` verdict and a non-null failure reason. Such states make policy decisions and serialization consumers unreliable.
findings.recommendation: Use one authoritative representation, such as an availability status discriminated union with a required reason for unavailable results, and derive the verdict or boolean rather than storing all three independently.

findings.title: SecurityScanResult contains multiple sources of truth
findings.description: `SecurityScanResult` stores the complete report alongside separate provenance, counts, and findings, even though the report already contains equivalent provenance fields, counters, and findings. Nothing ensures these copies agree, allowing consumers to observe different results depending on which property they read.
findings.recommendation: Choose one canonical shape. Prefer composing the report from `Provenance`, `Counts`, and `Findings`, or expose only `Report` and derive convenience views from it instead of accepting independent copies.

findings.title: Scan timestamps accept arbitrary strings
findings.description: Using `string` for `ScannedAt` permits malformed, ambiguous, and timezone-free values. Its nullability also differs between the report and provenance models, despite both apparently describing the same scan time.
findings.recommendation: Use `DateTimeOffset` consistently and define the intended JSON representation. If an absent timestamp is a valid state, make that choice consistent across both models.

grade.rationale: The API is compact, readable, and builds successfully according to the supplied analyzer evidence. Its main weaknesses are weakly typed provenance fields and registry construction that exposes incidental collection exceptions instead of clear domain validation.

observations.summary: The sensor abstractions are generally clear and maintainable, with sensible cancellation support and deterministic registry ordering. Strengthening provenance types and validating sensor registrations would prevent invalid metadata and improve startup diagnostics and testability. Test coverage is unknown.

findings.title: Provenance timestamps are stored as unvalidated strings
findings.description: `ScannedAt` accepts any string, so sensors can emit malformed timestamps, timestamps without an offset, or inconsistent formats. Consumers must repeatedly parse and validate the value, and chronological comparisons may be unreliable.
findings.recommendation: Represent the value as `DateTimeOffset` (or `Instant` if the project uses Noda Time), and serialize it in a standardized format only at persistence or transport boundaries.

findings.title: Provenance duplicates the typed scope as a free-form string
findings.description: The model defines `SensorScope` but stores provenance scope as `string`. This permits unsupported values and creates conversion code, spelling differences, and possible disagreement between the request scope and recorded provenance.
findings.recommendation: Change `SensorProvenance.Scope` to `SensorScope`; perform any required textual serialization at the system boundary.

findings.title: Registry construction relies on incidental dictionary exceptions
findings.description: The constructor does not explicitly validate the sensor sequence, entries, or IDs. A null entry causes a `NullReferenceException`, while duplicate IDs—including IDs differing only by case—cause a generic `ArgumentException`. These failures provide less actionable configuration diagnostics than the domain-specific lookup error.
findings.recommendation: Guard against a null collection, null entries, and null, empty, or whitespace IDs; detect case-insensitive duplicates explicitly and throw a dedicated registration/configuration exception that names the conflicting ID.

grade.rationale: The core freshness comparison is understandable and generally sound, and the available .NET build analyzer reported no findings. However, process I/O can deadlock, metadata validation has exception-handling gaps, file enumeration is not based on one consistent snapshot, and scan telemetry reports unsuccessful scans as completed.

observations.summary: The implementation has a clear high-level flow, useful cancellation propagation, and sensible path-containment checks. Its main risks are in Git subprocess management and malformed-metadata handling. Test coverage is unknown; the unavailable ESLint result is unrelated to this C# file.

findings.title: Sequentially reading redirected Git streams can deadlock
findings.description: The method drains standard output completely before reading standard error. If Git writes enough error output to fill the redirected stderr pipe while stdout is still being consumed, Git can block waiting for stderr space and never close stdout, leaving the scan hung.
findings.recommendation: Start reading stdout and stderr concurrently, then await both readers and process completion. Preserve cancellation behavior and ensure the child process is terminated and awaited when enumeration is cancelled or abandoned.

findings.title: Malformed metadata can escape as unexpected raw exceptions
findings.description: Required JSON strings are asserted with the null-forgiving operator and immediately passed to methods that dereference them. A JSON null for a path can therefore cause NullReferenceException, which is not wrapped by the catch filter. UnauthorizedAccessException from opening metadata is also omitted, so callers receive inconsistent exception types instead of the documented scan-level failure behavior implied by StalenessScanException.
findings.recommendation: Validate every required property for existence, JSON type, and non-empty string value before constructing ReviewMetadata. Convert schema failures and expected file-access failures, including UnauthorizedAccessException, into StalenessScanException with the metadata path and a useful cause.

findings.title: Metadata and subjects are collected from separate Git enumerations
findings.description: The first Git invocation supplies metadata, while a second invocation supplies subjects. If files are added, removed, or renamed between those invocations, the report can pair subjects with a different metadata snapshot and incorrectly report reviews as missing or omit files. It also doubles subprocess and traversal cost.
findings.recommendation: Materialize one normalized file list from a single Git invocation, then use that same snapshot both to load metadata and to evaluate subjects.

findings.title: Failed and cancelled scans are logged as completed
findings.description: ScanCompleted is emitted from a finally block, so it runs even when metadata parsing, Git enumeration, hashing, input resolution, or cancellation terminates the scan. The event contains no outcome field and its file count may be partial, which can make operational telemetry falsely indicate success.
findings.recommendation: Emit ScanCompleted only after successful completion, or replace it with a terminal event that includes an explicit success, failure, or cancellation outcome and clearly labels partial counts.

findings.title: Git and filesystem dependencies cannot be substituted in tests
findings.description: Although InputResolver is injectable, the evaluator directly uses Process, File, and Directory throughout. Tests for Git startup failures, blocked streams, cancellation, access errors, and changing file snapshots therefore require real operating-system state and timing, making them slower and less deterministic.
findings.recommendation: Introduce narrow abstractions for repository file enumeration and metadata/content access, keeping production implementations backed by Git and System.IO. Inject those abstractions so unit tests can model failures and races deterministically.

grade.rationale: The models are concise and readable, and the derived freshness logic is straightforward. The main weakness is that collection-valued records do not provide stable immutable snapshots or true value-based equality, despite otherwise presenting as immutable value objects.

observations.summary: Well-structured model definitions with one maintainability and correctness concern around collection ownership and record equality. No test coverage conclusions can be drawn from the supplied evidence, and the successful .NET build reported no analyzer findings for this file.

findings.title: Collection-valued records are neither immutable snapshots nor structurally comparable
findings.description: `StalenessReport` and `StalenessEvaluatorOptions` store `IReadOnlyList<T>` references directly. That interface prevents mutation through the declared property but does not prevent callers from retaining and mutating the underlying list or array, so counts and option behavior can change after construction. In addition, generated record equality compares these collections using their own equality implementation, which is normally reference equality; two otherwise identical instances containing independently created lists therefore compare unequal, and `with` copies share the same collection reference.
findings.recommendation: Use an immutable collection type such as `ImmutableArray<T>` and defensively materialize incoming sequences. If these types are not intended to have structural value equality, consider ordinary sealed classes instead of records; otherwise implement explicit sequence-based equality and hashing.

grade.rationale: The enum is concise, idiomatic, and internally consistent. No correctness, maintainability, clarity, error-handling, or testability defects are evident from the supplied file.

observations.summary: No actionable issues were identified. The public enum clearly represents four distinct staleness states, and the available .NET build evidence reports no findings. Test coverage remains unknown and does not affect the assessment.

grade.rationale: The implementation is compact and readable, but concurrent access from separate processes can cause append or query failures, and accepted entries are not validated for basic numeric invariants. Silent corruption handling and permanently retained locks further weaken operability and maintainability.

observations.summary: The ledger has a clear data model and straightforward aggregation logic. Its main risk is that synchronization is process-local while the ledger is repository-local, making ordinary multi-process use unreliable. Validation and corruption observability also need strengthening.

findings.title: Process-local locking does not make repository ledger access safe
findings.description: The semaphore coordinates only callers within the current process. Another process appending to the same monthly file can race and receive an IOException because the writer does not share write access. A simultaneous query can also conflict because File.ReadLinesAsync normally opens its reader without sharing writes. Concurrent CLI or agent processes can therefore lose an attempted telemetry append or fail a report query.
findings.recommendation: Introduce cross-process coordination, such as an OS-visible lock file or named mutex scoped to the canonical ledger path, and define compatible reader/writer sharing. Add bounded retry handling for transient sharing violations and tests that exercise concurrent readers and writers from separate processes.

findings.title: Schema validation accepts negative token counts and durations
findings.description: IsSupported validates required strings and schema relationships but accepts negative token counts and DurationMs values. Such entries are persisted and subsequently subtract from aggregate totals, violating the semantic meaning of usage measurements.
findings.recommendation: Reject negative DurationMs and negative non-null token fields before appending. Consider centralizing these invariants in a validated factory or constructor so invalid entries cannot be created accidentally.

findings.title: Corrupt ledger records are silently omitted from reports
findings.description: Catching JsonException allows later records to remain readable, but no warning, error count, or diagnostic callback reveals that data was discarded. Reports can consequently undercount usage while appearing complete, making persistent corruption difficult to detect or investigate.
findings.recommendation: Continue processing after malformed lines, but expose corruption through logging or report diagnostics containing at least the file and line number. Avoid including sensitive line contents in diagnostics.

findings.title: Per-ledger semaphores are retained for the lifetime of the process
findings.description: Every distinct canonical repository/month path creates a SemaphoreSlim that remains in the static dictionary permanently. Long-lived processes operating across many repositories or months accumulate unused synchronization objects without a bound.
findings.recommendation: Use a reference-counted keyed-lock abstraction that safely removes idle entries, or scope lock ownership to a shorter-lived ledger service instance. Ensure removal cannot race with queued callers.

grade.rationale: The runner is readable and builds successfully, but repository-boundary enforcement is incomplete, failures are not isolated by analysis, and extensibility and repeated hashing concerns can produce incorrect or unnecessarily fragile behavior.

observations.summary: The implementation has a clear request/result model and straightforward control flow. The principal risk is that path-scoped analyses receive caller-provided paths without repository containment checks. Additional issues affect failure isolation, classification of custom sensors, hashing efficiency, and deterministic testing. Coverage is unknown; the supplied build analyzer reported no findings, while ESLint was unavailable for an unrelated missing dependency.

findings.title: Path-scoped analyses are not confined to the repository
findings.description: A path-scoped definition is checked only for a non-empty path and is then passed directly to the sensor. An absolute path or a path containing parent traversal can therefore direct a sensor outside RepositoryPath, contrary to the repository-scoped contract and potentially expose unrelated files to external analysis tools.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the requested path against the canonical repository root before invoking a sensor, reject rooted paths when repository-relative paths are required, and verify that the resolved target is the root or a descendant using platform-appropriate path comparison. Consider resolving links as well when strict containment is required.

findings.title: One sensor failure aborts the entire analysis batch
findings.description: The sensor invocation has no runner-level failure boundary. Any non-cancellation exception discards results from analyses that already completed, prevents subsequent analyses from running, and may reach the caller without identifying which named analysis failed.
findings.recommendation: Define an explicit batch-failure policy. For resilient batch execution, catch non-cancellation exceptions per sensor and record a failed or unavailable execution with useful context; otherwise wrap and rethrow with the sensor ID while preserving the original exception. Always allow cancellation exceptions to propagate.

findings.title: Review kind is hard-coded from two sensor IDs
findings.description: Every sensor other than gitleaks and dependencies is classified as code. An injected or future security sensor will consequently emit envelopes with ReviewKind.Code even when its findings are security findings, making the public sensor-injection extension point semantically incorrect.
findings.recommendation: Make review kind part of the sensor contract or finding metadata and use that declared value when constructing the subject. If a fallback is necessary, validate it explicitly rather than inferring semantics from sensor names.

findings.title: File content is rehashed for every finding
findings.description: ToEnvelopeAsync computes the subject hash independently for each finding. When many findings point to the same file, the runner repeatedly opens and hashes identical content, causing avoidable I/O and potentially substantial run-time growth for large files or result sets.
findings.recommendation: Normalize the subject path and cache the hash once per file for the duration of RunAsync, ideally as a dictionary of lazily created tasks so repeated findings share both successful work and cancellation behavior.

findings.title: Direct system-clock access prevents deterministic timestamps
findings.description: Run timestamps are read directly from DateTimeOffset.UtcNow. Tests must assert broad time ranges and cannot reliably verify exact timestamps, elapsed ordering, or clock-related edge cases.
findings.recommendation: Inject a TimeProvider, defaulting to TimeProvider.System, and obtain both timestamps from it. Tests can then use a fixed or controllable provider.
